sources.news_title: US Army set to detonate ageing explosives despite risk of toxic fallout
sources.text:
US Army set to detonate ageing explosives despite risk of toxic fallout
The US Army has set off waves of anxiety in Iowa after it confirmed plans to carry out two controlled explosions at an ammunition facility there with just a few days’ notice – and it has invoked emergency provisions to avoid a court order that had put its plans on hold.
According to the Army, dozens of old barrels containing degraded lead azide, an explosive used as a detonator, have become unstable and pose an “unacceptable risk of accidental detonation”. The Army says intentionally blowing up the barrels is the best option for controlling the risk.
However, the explosions are expected to release a large plume of lead particles, and lead is a neurotoxin. The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is in Middletown, a town of about 360 residents in south-east Iowa. People and farms would be in the path of the plume as the wind blows it for kilometres.
The detonations were briefly delayed after a backlash and rescheduled for November 23. A federal appeals court separately paused the Army’s emergency Environmental Protection Agency permit for the detonations after two groups sued, but the US Justice Department argued that the permit wasn’t necessary in the face of an immediate threat.
The Justice Department told the court in a response late on November 21 that the Army intended to carry out the detonations by November 24. A precise date and time weren’t immediately released.
The Army had hired a firm in March to use chemicals to neutralise the munitions, The New York Times reports, but it later cancelled the contract, citing safety concerns. The lead azide is in 68 drums weighing about 4440 kilograms. Having people handle the explosives increased the risk of accidental detonation, the Army said in documents.
The Iowa base plays a critical role in the nation’s defence as the main facility for loading explosives into artillery and mortar shells used by the Pentagon, The Times reports.
With all the concern, Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa, explained the risks people in the region would face. O’Shaughnessy is part of a team scrambling to have testing in place when the Army carries out its detonation plan.
What risks do the Army’s planned explosions pose for people?
If you picture a dust plume, it carries particulate matter that can get into the lungs as you breathe. In this case, we’re talking about small particles that contain lead, which is toxic to humans and pets.
Those particles will settle over the area downwind of the detonation site. First, it’s air pollution – if you’re outside, you can inhale those particles. Then it becomes surface pollution. The lead dust can get on your hands and into your body. The big concern there is for young children. If you think about two-year-olds, they put everything in their mouths.
Lead is easily absorbed by the body. It gets into the bloodstream and it can cause harm to just about every major organ in our bodies, including the nervous system and the brain. It tends to hide out in bones and teeth, where it can leach out and cause harm.
Studies have shown lead exposure is a major concern for pregnant women with developing fetuses. In young children, lead exposure can slow their brain development. Longstanding results from studies have demonstrated a reduction in IQ in children with chronic lead exposure, such as from lead-based paint in old houses.
The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention says there is no safe level of lead in the body. That’s a pretty strong statement.
What’s known about where the plume is likely to travel?
Where this plume travels and how far depends primarily on the wind speed and direction in the hours after the explosions.
We have a sense of what happens from studying pollution from smokestacks. Chimneys are tall for a reason – they eject the pollutants high into the atmosphere so the pollutants dilute as they drift downwind.
In this case, instead of a steady stream coming out of the smokestack, it’s going to be a big puff that will literally create a cloud. That cloud will rise and start dissipating as it is diluted in the air. It will become invisible at some point, but that doesn’t mean the lead isn’t there.
If the Army had blown up those storage containers on November 20, as initially planned, the forecast was for a fairly strong 15-mile-per-hour surface wind. The plume would have mostly diluted by the time it reached I-80, which is where I’m sitting, about 80 miles to the north.
If the Army goes through with its rescheduled plan on November 23, the preliminary forecast is for much slower wind blowing toward the south-southeast. Slower wind means the plume would affect a smaller area, but people there would experience a higher concentration of lead as it slowly floats by.
That may mean fewer people are affected, but the exposure could be more intense. We won’t know exactly what people will experience until it happens.
What can people do to stay safe in those areas?
Honestly, I would find a way to get out of the area for the day. If you can’t leave, the Army has a list of precautions that people should take, and I think those are good recommendations.
The Army is advising people near the plant to vacate their homes during the detonation and others to shelter in place. That means staying indoors and closing all your doors and windows. If you can, shut off the furnace – it pulls in air that could be contaminated as the plume travels through an area.
Within a few hours, the plume will have dissipated or moved on. But that doesn’t mean the lead disappears. It falls to the ground, meaning you and your pets can still get it on you.
After the plume dissipates, the Army suggests getting a hose and spraying down window sills, cars, any horizontal surfaces where the dust can accumulate. Car door handles can easily collect and transfer the lead to people. If you have children’s play areas or toys outside, wash those down.
Lead is a persistent compound – there’s no way to degrade it. Washing it off surfaces transfers the lead to the soil. At this point in the year, the majority of the crops have been harvested, so there’s less risk of lead settling on plants in farm fields. However, some dairy farmers are concerned about their cows getting into lead that settles on grass.
Our results from sampling during and after the plume should help people better understand the risks.
What is your team planning for testing?
My colleagues and I will be looking at two aspects of potential exposure to lead: the airborne dust, which we’ll collect with instruments during the plume to get the lead concentration, and then dust that settles on surfaces and the ground, which we’ll collect with gauzelike pads and send to a lab for analysis.
The lab will be able to tell how much lead is in those samples, and the air samples will let us calculate how much people were exposed to the lead.
This is all happening last minute – we only found out about the plan a few days before the Army initially planned to detonate the barrels. Thankfully, the university and our federal- and state-funded centres have the people and technology to quickly carry out testing. We hope to have results about a week after it happens. The US Environmental Protection Agency also has a team that will be doing sampling.
This interview was originally published in The Conversation.

sources.news_title: Trump admin tells court it will blow up a toxic stockpile in the heartland — permit or not
sources.text:
The U.S. Justice Department on Sunday urged a federal appeals court to lift the administrative stay on a permit that would allow the Army to detonate 9,700 pounds of a lead-based explosive in southeast Iowa.
The DOJ arguments came the same day that environmental groups in the court case filed affidavits from scientists and officials who argued against the Army’s reasons to go ahead with the detonation, which the government said would occur on Nov. 24.
While the lawsuit and stay ordered by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit focus on an emergency permit issued by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, the DOJ informed the court late Saturday that the Army intends to invoke an exclusion to the law allowing it to detonate without the permit.
The DOJ’s Sunday filing opposing the environmental groups’ motion on the permit emphasized that a controlled detonation of the lead azide was “necessary now to respond to the immediate threat of an uncontrolled explosion at” the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown.
“EPA’s regulations allow the Army’s planned action without the need for a permit, and the Army intends to act on November 24, 2026,” the filing said.
A public affairs contact with the U.S. Army did not respond immediately Sunday to a request for confirmation of the new detonation date.
The lead azide, located at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, was originally set for detonation on Nov. 20, then was pushed back to Nov. 23 amid concern from the public and the lawsuit.
As of Sunday afternoon, the Army had not posted updated models for the new detonation date, nor announced an official schedule since the original postponement was announced.
A Sunday news release from the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club Iowa Chapter and Earthjustice – the environmental groups suing over the EPA petition – criticized the lack of public information as the Army intends to move forward.
“The Army has clearly mishandled this situation, and Iowans and residents in our neighboring states deserve a full review of all of the missteps that led us to this point,” Sierra Club Iowa Chapter Legal Chair Wally Taylor said in the release. “However, if detonation is now the only option, it is imperative that everyone impacted has access to the full range of testing, mitigation, and remediation resources.”
What outside scientists said
In its filing Saturday night, the DOJ said the Army intends to detonate regardless of the court stay because of the “immediate risk” that the degraded lead azide “will explode” when temperatures drop in the next several days.
A declaration from an Army munitions expert informed the court that changes in temperature can further destabilize the lead azide by causing more crystallization.
One of the scientists who filed affidavits supporting the environmental groups’ requests to halt the detonation, challenged this point, arguing the barrels were insulated from drastic temperature changes by the earthen structures the Army had put up around the material.
Mark Thomas, an environmental health science researcher who formerly worked for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, argued in his affidavit that the anticipated drop in temperature, which the Army has cited as a reason to go ahead with the detonation, “would not translate into an immediate or comparable change in temperature inside the earth covered magazines where the material is stored.”
Another scientist, Ranajit Sahu, a “combustion and heat transfer expert” and consultant, said he “cannot rule out the potential formation and release of a wider range of combustion toxics” in addition to the lead, when the lead azide is detonated.
“Given the lack of detail provided to the public, it is clear that the potential for release of such dangerous chemicals and their impacts have not been fully assessed in planning for this detonation,” Sahu said in his filing.
He also emphasized that the option to chemically neutralize the lead azide was “hastily rejected” by EPA and the Army. In a filing late Saturday, DOJ said even removing the lids of the barrels to administer a chemical for treatment posed too great a risk for spontaneous detonation.
Concerns in Iowa City
Iowa City City Manager Geoff Fruin also submitted a declaration stating residents have voiced concerns to the city, which sits about 62 miles northwest of Middletown, about air quality, residual lead and the potential for short and long-term health impacts.
The city has received no formal notification of the detonation beyond a Nov. 20 email letting Fruin know about the deployment of an EPA team to gather a pre-detonation surface water sample, as the city sits within a 100-mile radius of the detonation zone, he said.
The Iowa City Water Treatment Plant produces around 6 million gallons of drinking water daily, Fruin stated, with a raw water source in the Iowa River and distributions across the city, University Heights and other nearby areas. The city is concerned about impacts to the river, as well as those to the “several thousand children aged six and under” and around 12,850 people ages 65 and up living in the area.
“Iowa City has been discussing possible protocols to address impacts from the detonation; however, it is difficult due to the lack of notice and information that has been provided,” Fruin said in his declaration. “The City of Iowa City supports the Iowa Environmental Council and Iowa Sierra Club in taking legal action to ensure that the lead azide is disposed of safely, with adequate and accurate information provided to allow the public to prepare, with adequate follow-up and support for any post-detonation impacts, and with a minimum of harm to the environment and population.”
Some residents in Middletown have said they’d rather the Army go ahead with the detonation than risk an unplanned detonation, according to reporting.
A separate Sunday filing from the DOJ, on behalf of the EPA, which is named in the lawsuit, opposed the environmental groups’ request to add the testimonies to the record, stating they were made after the EPA’s permit decision and sit “plainly outside the record for judicial review.”
DOJ urges court to end the administrative stay
The DOJ responded in opposition to the environmental groups’ request to pause and reevaluate an emergency permit issued by EPA allowing the Army to intentionally detonate the degraded explosives.
The DOJ argues environmental groups didn’t fully demonstrate that a stay would “serve the public interest” nor their likelihood for success in the motion.
In the initial filing, environmental groups acknowledged the risk involved in leaving the lead azide at the IAAAP untreated, though they argued about the EPA’s determination that detonation was the best course of action. DOJ pointed to this in its most recent filing.
“Petitioners do not challenge that determination. Instead, they ask this Court to second-guess the agencies’ technical judgments about the specific permit terms needed to protect human health and the environment during a controlled detonation,” DOJ said.
DOJ emphasized that a controlled detonation, as determined by EPA and the Army, is the best method to avert “a more damaging uncontrolled explosion.”
“Petitioners cannot show that the public will not be harmed if the Permit is stayed,” the DOJ said.
In a news conference Friday, Taylor, with the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter, said it was a “lame excuse,” considering the material had been sitting in the Middletown plant for decades.
Much of the public concern centers around the release of lead particles into the air with the detonation, as lead is toxic to humans and animals.
The DOJ brief said the environmental groups fault EPA for “authorizing any release of lead dust.”
“But no option prevents every release here; the only choice is between a release the Army can manage and one it cannot,” DOJ said.
The government argues the EPA permit was “reasonable” and that the environmental groups are “not likely to prevail” in their request for a stay of the permit. The DOJ urges the court to lift the administrative stay and deny environmental groups’ motion.
“The Army has delayed detonation by three days now,” the filing said. “But every day of delay increases the risk of an uncontrolled explosion that will cause far greater public health and environmental harm than the planned, controlled detonation initiated under the protective terms of the Permit.”

sources.news_title: US Army plans to invoke emergency provisions to detonate bomb-making chemicals in Iowa - WSVN 7News | Miami News, Weather, Sports
sources.text:
The U.S. Army plans to invoke emergency provisions to avoid a court order that had put on hold plans to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa, saying that continued delays will make it more dangerous as the weather starts to turn colder.
“To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action,” government lawyers told the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in a filing late Saturday. “Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay.”
The Army plans to detonate the chemicals by Tuesday.
Environmental groups criticized the government’s move, decrying it as a maneuver to get around a court order and avoid public demands for safety and transparency.
The appeals court on Thursday granted a request by environmentalists to put on hold a permit that cleared the way for the detonation in Middletown, a small community about 160 miles (257 kilometers) southeast of Des Moines. It was initially planned for Friday, but the Army later announced that it would push the operation to Monday following an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.
Environmentalists have called for a review of the emergency permit that was approved earlier this month by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
In a statement Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club, and Earthjustice questioned claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration.
“The Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public’s demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm,” said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau.
Government lawyers said the Army doesn’t need a permit to take emergency action against an immediate threat from explosive material.
They said the standards of a federal law regulating hazardous waste don’t apply in situations when there’s an immediate threat to health, safety or the environment as determined by an explosive or munitions emergency response specialist.
Officials contend that the chemicals are unstable, and the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop. They said there is a risk that the chemicals may explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1 Celsius) in the coming days.
In March, staff at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant found several dozen barrels of degraded lead azide, which is used in munitions production. Crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the Army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan.
According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums’ contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.
The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their petition that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public.
The Army had shared details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, but a public advisory a week ago was the first time other communities — some as far away as 100 miles (160 kilometers) — became aware of the potential impact. Nearly 400 people live in Middletown but thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground.
Vibrations from the two planned blasts were expected to be quick, but they could break old windows. That led officials to recommend some residents in Middletown vacate the area.
Iowans in the region were told to stay inside; keep windows and doors closed; bring pets and livestock indoors; and clean cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces afterward.
“The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory states. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals.”

Army plans to detonate degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown Tuesday. In a response filed Sunday, officials said the material has been deteriorating for years, forming crystals that are extremely sensitive to movement, friction and temperature changes.

sources.news_title: Environmental groups say legal status of planned lead detonation in Iowa remains uncertain
sources.text:
A Sierra Club attorney said Sunday it remains unclear whether a court order temporarily putting on hold the Army’s EPA permit would prevent the Army from detonating nearly five tons of lead azide Monday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.
The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals issued an administrative stay of the EPA’s emergency permit Thursday, pending its ruling on the groups’ emergency motion. That prompted the federal government to say it would use its emergency authority to continue with its plan to destroy the chemicals being stored south of the Quad-Cities and near the Mississippi River.
The Army had planned to detonate the material Friday, then announced a delay until Monday, the Associated Press reported.
In a notice filed late Saturday, the U.S. Justice Department said the Army intends to invoke a separate emergency exclusion under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) to detonate the material without a permit from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency EPA permit no later than Nov. 24.
The federal government argues the court’s administrative stay of the EPA permit does not prevent the Army from acting under a separate RCRA emergency exclusion. The government said colder weather and continued delays could increase the danger, according to AP.
Wally Taylor, legal chair for the Sierra Club’s Iowa Chapter, said the groups fighting to halt the detonation believe the court’s stay should stop the demolition, while the Army argues the order does not apply to action under the separate authority its invoking.
“I guess a lawyer’s answer is we don’t know. It’s a little up in the air,” Taylor said.
The Sierra Club is still asking the court to extend the stay, he said, though he is not confident the court can prevent the Army from acting.
” It’s been really discouraging that the Army has not been more transparent about what they’re doing and when they let people know,” Taylor said. “We didn’t know about this until just a few days ago, and the Army apparently has known about this for quite some time, but they haven’t been very good about notifying the public.”
He said his group and others want the demolition to be done safely and be followed by adequate cleanup if it proceeds.
The environmental groups said in a Sunday statement that declarations filed with the court challenged the Army’s public notice and questioned whether it had properly considered alternatives.
The groups have urged consideration of chemical neutralization, though the Army says that option would require prolonged handling of the 68 drums and increase the risk of an accidental explosion, the AP reported.
Cody Smith, program director at the Iowa Environmental Council, said the council had not received updated plume maps or modeling and was urging the Army to release them.
“We are less than 48 hours from their planned date of detonation according to the filing today, and we have yet to see any of that information,” Smith said. “It’s critical for Iowans and community leaders at every level to be able to protect themselves and their families from lead exposure, of which we know there is no safe level for humans.”
Smith said the filings led the environmental council to believe detonation may now be the best treatment option, but he blamed the Army’s handling and storage of the material for creating the crisis.
He said the Army had not directly confirmed a date or time. Although the filings indicate a plan to act by Tuesday, he said the timing remained unconfirmed.
” I think it’s really important that folks continue to call on the Army and on federal officials for transparency as soon as possible,” Smith said. “If folks are looking for something to do, reaching out to their elected federal officials is probably the most helpful at this point.”

sources.news_title: Army plans to detonate several tons of unstable explosives at Iowa munitions plant by Tuesday
sources.text:
The U.S. Army plans to move forward with detonating tons of unstable lead azide sitting in an Iowa munitions plant despite a federal court order temporarily blocking the detonation.
The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, contains 68 drums of lead azide that has crystallized, degrading the five tons of explosives used in detonators to the point where they are in danger of exploding at any time, according to the U.S. government. The Army had planned to detonate the lead azide on Friday in accordance with a permit from the Environmental Protection Agency, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit issued a short-term stay, blocking the detonation.
Recommended Stories
Despite the court-ordered stay, the federal government stated it planned to move forward with it anyway. The Department of Justice wrote in a court filing on Sunday that a controlled detonation of the substance is “the only way to minimize the release” of lead dust.
“The choice therefore is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned detonation (timed for favorable weather, preceded by public notice, and followed by monitoring and cleanup) and an unplanned explosion that could come at any moment, with no warning and no safeguards,” the Justice Department lawyers wrote in the filing.
The detonation operation was initially scheduled for Friday, Nov. 20, but the Army had delayed it until Monday before the court-ordered stay on Thursday. The court filing announced the newly planned detonation date of Tuesday, Nov. 24.
“A controlled detonation is necessary now to respond to the immediate threat of an uncontrolled explosion at the Facility. EPA’s regulations allow the Army’s planned action without the need for a permit, and the Army intends to act on November 24, 2026,” the lawyers wrote in the filing.
MIDWEST GOVERNORS REASSURE PUBLIC AS ARMY PLANS IOWA LEAD EXPLOSION
The detonation is time-sensitive, according to the Army, because forecasted cold weather could make the explosive substance even more volatile and in danger of an unpredictable explosion.
The Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club, and concerned local citizens worry about a detonation under any circumstances and the possibility of the spread of aerosolized lead throughout their community. The groups have voiced concerns about both the public health and environmental impact of the explosion.

sources.news_title: US Army to detonate toxic lead in Iowa despite court's temporary freeze
sources.text:
The US Army will detonate 68 barrels of toxic lead azide in Iowa by Tuesday under emergency legal powers that allow it to bypass a court order blocking the controversial plan, the Trump administration told a court this weekend.
The US Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit temporarily halted the detonation by freezing the Army’s environmental permit on Thursday after environmental groups sued to halt the operation.
In Saturday night's filing, the government said the Army plans to move forward without a permit by invoking an emergency munitions and explosives exception to federal environmental protection laws.
Threat of uncontrolled explosion
“The Army must perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion, and the Army intends to act by November 24, 2026,” the Justice Department said in a court filing late on Saturday.
Federal officials say the detonation must go forward within the next several days because a drop in temperature could destabilize the material and cause an uncontrolled explosion.
The Army previously postponed plans to detonate the degraded lead azide, an explosive used in military munitions, after public outcry by residents and farmers near Middletown, Iowa.
The Army did not immediately respond to an inquiry on Sunday about the precise timing of the detonation.
The Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club's Iowa chapter filed the lawsuit.
Army seems more concerned with avoiding 'judicial process, ' nonprofit argues
Earthjustice, a nonprofit environmental law organization suing on behalf of the groups, said in a statement on Sunday that the Army seems more concerned with "finding a way to sidestep the judicial process" than meeting public demands for greater transparency and protection from the detonation's potential fallout.
The plaintiffs have argued that the detonations would release a toxic plume of lead dust into the air that could travel 100 miles (161 kilometers) north of the site, depending on weather conditions.
Lead exposure can cause serious health problems, particularly in children, including damage to the brain and nervous system.
In a statement on Thursday, acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the Army had determined with the US Environmental Protection Agency that a controlled detonation to dispose of the degraded lead was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public.
Still, the Army advised people to avoid the affected area during the detonation and urged anyone who could not leave beforehand to stay indoors, close windows and doors, and shut off heating and cooling systems that bring in outside air. Residents should wet-clean surfaces children may touch to remove any lead dust once the exposure period has ended, the Army said.
The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship has recommended that cattle farmers near the detonation site move their livestock, feed, and equipment to alternate locations or indoors.

(THE CONVERSATION) The U.S. Army set off waves of anxiety in Iowa when it confirmed plans to carry out two controlled explosions at an ammunition facility there with just a few days’ notice. According to the Army, dozens of old barrels containing lead azide, an explosive used as a detonator, have become unstable and pose an “unacceptable risk of accidental detonation.” Intentionally detonating the barrels is considered the best option for controlling the risk, the Army determined.
However, the explosions are expected to release a large plume of lead particles, and lead is a neurotoxin. The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is in Middletown, a town of about 360 residents in southeast Iowa. People and farms would be in the path of the plume as the wind blows it for miles.
The detonations were briefly delayed after the backlash and rescheduled for Nov. 23, 2026. A federal appeals court separately paused the Army’s emergency Environmental Protection Agency permit for the detonations after two groups sued, but the U.S. Justice Department argued that the permit wasn’t necessary in the face of an immediate threat.
The Justice Department told the court in a response late on Nov. 21 that the Army intends to carry out the detonations by Nov. 24, 2026. A precise date and time weren’t immediately released.
To better understand the risks, we asked Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa, what people in the region would face. O'Shaughnessy is part of a team scrambling to have testing in place when the Army carries out its detonation plan.
What risks do the Army’s planned explosions pose for people?
If you picture a dust plume, it carries particulate matter that can get into the lungs as you breathe. In this case, we’re talking about small particles that contain lead, which is toxic to humans and pets.
Those particles will settle over the area downwind of the detonation site. First it’s air pollution – if you’re outside, you can inhale those particles. Then it becomes surface pollution. The lead dust can get on your hands and into your body. The big concern there is for young children. If you think about 2-year-olds, they put everything in their mouths.
Lead is easily absorbed by the body. It gets into the bloodstream, and it can cause harm to just about every major organ in our bodies, including the nervous system and the brain. It tends to hide out in bones and teeth, where it can leach out and cause harm.
Studies have shown lead exposure is a major concern for pregnant women with developing fetuses. In young children, lead exposure can slow their brain development. Long-standing results from studies have demonstrated a reduction in IQ in children with chronic lead exposure, such as from lead-based paint in old houses.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says there is no safe level of lead in the body. That’s a pretty strong statement.
What’s known about where the plume is likely to travel?
Where this plume travels and how far depends primarily on the wind speed and direction in the hours after the explosions.
We have a sense of what happens from studying pollution from smokestacks. Smokestacks are tall for a reason – they eject the pollutants high into the atmosphere so the pollutants dilute as they drift downwind.
In this case, instead of a steady stream coming out of the smokestack, it’s going to be a big puff that will literally create a cloud. That cloud will rise and start dissipating as it is diluted in the air. It will become invisible at some point, but that doesn’t mean the lead isn’t there.
If the Army had blown up those storage containers on Nov. 20, as initially planned, the forecast was for a fairly strong 15-mile-per-hour surface wind. The plume would have mostly diluted by the time it reached I-80, which is where I’m sitting, about 80 miles to the north.
If the Army goes through with its rescheduled plan on Nov. 23, the preliminary forecast is for much slower wind blowing toward the south-southeast. Slower wind means the plume would affect a smaller area, but people there would experience a higher concentration of lead as it slowly floats by.
That may mean fewer people are affected, but the exposure could be more intense. We won’t know exactly what people will experience until it happens.
What can people do to stay safe in those areas?
Honestly, I would find a way to get out of the area for the day. If you can’t leave, the Army has a list of precautions that people should take, and I think those are good recommendations.
The Army is advising people near the plant to vacate their homes during the detonation and others to shelter in place. That means staying indoors and closing all your doors and windows. If you can, shut off the furnace – it pulls in air that could be contaminated as the plume travels through an area.
Within a few hours, the plume will have dissipated or moved on. But that doesn’t mean the lead disappears. It falls to the ground, meaning you and your pets can still get it on you.
After the plumed dissipates, the Army suggests getting a hose and spraying down window sills, cars, any horizontal surfaces where the dust can accumulate. Car door handles can easily collect and transfer the lead to people. If you have children’s play areas or toys outside, wash those down.
Lead is a persistent compound – there’s no way to degrade it. Washing it off surfaces transfers the lead to the soil. At this point in the year, the majority of the crops have been harvested, so there’s less risk of lead settling on plants in farm fields. However, some dairy farmers are concerned about their cows getting into lead that settles on grass.
Our results from sampling during and after the plume should help people better understand the risks.
What is your team planning for testing?
My colleagues and I will be looking at two aspects of potential exposure to lead: the airborne dust, which we’ll collect with instruments during the plume to get the lead concentration, and then dust that settles on surfaces and the ground, which we’ll collect with gauzelike pads and send to a lab for analysis.
The lab will be able to tell how much lead is in those samples, and the air samples will let us calculate how much people were exposed to the lead.
This is all happening last minute – we only found out about the plan a few days before the Army initially planned to detonate the barrels. Thankfully, the university and our federal- and state-fundedcenters have the people and technology to quickly carry out testing. We hope to have results about a week after it happens. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also has a team that will be doing sampling.

sources.news_title: U.S. Army to perform detonation at Iowa munitions plant by Tuesday
US Army plans to invoke emergency provisions to detonate bomb-making chemicals in Iowa
sources.text:
The U.S. Army plans to invoke emergency provisions to avoid a court order that had put on hold plans to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa, saying that continued delays will make it more dangerous as the weather starts to turn colder.
“To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action,” government lawyers told the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in a filing late Saturday. “Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay.”
The Army plans to detonate the chemicals by Tuesday.
Environmental groups criticized the government’s move, decrying it as a maneuver to get around a court order and avoid public demands for safety and transparency.
The appeals court on Thursday granted a request by environmentalists to put on hold a permit that cleared the way for the detonation in Middletown, a small community about 160 miles (257 kilometers) southeast of Des Moines. It was initially planned for Friday, but the Army later announced that it would push the operation to Monday following an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.
Environmentalists have called for a review of the emergency permit that was approved earlier this month by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
In a statement Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club, and Earthjustice questioned claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration.
“The Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public’s demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm,” said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau.
Government lawyers said the Army doesn’t need a permit to take emergency action against an immediate threat from explosive material.
They said the standards of a federal law regulating hazardous waste don’t apply in situations when there’s an immediate threat to health, safety or the environment as determined by an explosive or munitions emergency response specialist.
Officials contend that the chemicals are unstable, and the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop. They said there is a risk that the chemicals may explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1 Celsius) in the coming days.
In March, staff at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant found several dozen barrels of degraded lead azide, which is used in munitions production. Crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the Army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan.
According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums’ contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.
The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their petition that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public.
The Army had shared details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, but a public advisory a week ago was the first time other communities — some as far away as 100 miles (160 kilometers) — became aware of the potential impact. Nearly 400 people live in Middletown but thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground.
Vibrations from the two planned blasts were expected to be quick, but they could break old windows. That led officials to recommend some residents in Middletown vacate the area.
Iowans in the region were told to stay inside; keep windows and doors closed; bring pets and livestock indoors; and clean cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces afterward.
“The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory states. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals.”

sources.news_title: Army says it will detonate lead azide in Iowa under emergency exclusion, despite court order
sources.text:
The U.S. Army plans to detonate 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, without a permit, invoking an emergency exception to federal environmental law after a federal appeals court froze the permit it had been granted.
The two controlled detonations are expected to go off at approximately noon Monday, according to the Army.
“The Army must perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion, and the Army intends to act by November 24, 2026,” the Justice Department said in a court filing late Saturday.
The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily halted the detonation Thursday by staying the Army’s U.S. Environmental Protection Agency permit. The Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club’s Iowa chapter had sued to stop the operation. Earthjustice, a nonprofit environmental law organization, represents the groups.
In a statement Thursday, acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said the Army and the EPA had determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public.
The plaintiffs argue the detonations would release a toxic plume of lead dust that could travel 100 miles north of the site, depending on weather. Lead exposure can cause serious health problems, particularly in children, including damage to the brain and nervous system.
The Army had already postponed the detonation once, from noon Friday to Monday, after outcry from residents and farmers near Middletown. The court order came after that.
Iowa and Illinois officials, including Gov. JB Pritzker, had called for the Army to postpone the detonation to find a safer alternative, voicing alarm about the potential for lead to harm humans and the environment around the site.
In Saturday’s filing, the government said the Army would proceed under the “emergency munitions and explosives exclusion” to the EPA’s regulatory processes.
Before the filing, Earthjustice attorney Thien Chau said the bar for the emergency exception is very high.
“You have to show that there is no other possible safe alternative for treating this,” he said.
The Army says the lead azide, which is used to make blasting caps, has degraded. The material is stored in water and has recrystallized, making it volatile and vulnerable to an accidental explosion. It has been stored at the site for almost two decades, the Army said.
Temperatures in Iowa are expected to drop below 30 degrees this week, the Army said in its filing, raising the risk.
“As the outside temperatures drop, the risk of an uncontrolled explosion increases because the formed crystals can break more easily in freezing temperatures,” the filing said.
Under the Army’s plan, the lead azide will be detonated inside earth-covered concrete magazines surrounded by sand barriers about two stories high. The soil above the magazines will be saturated and sprayed with water before and during the blast.
Citing its own predictive models, the Army said those measures will keep airborne lead “well below” the level that would require the EPA to take additional action.
The Army advised people to avoid the area during the detonation. Anyone who cannot leave beforehand should stay indoors, close windows and doors, and shut off heating and cooling systems that bring in outside air, the Army said. Once the exposure period ends, residents should wet-clean surfaces children may touch to remove any lead dust.
The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship has recommended that cattle farmers near the site move livestock, feed and equipment to other locations or indoors.
The Army plans to evacuate areas immediately next to the site, all in Iowa, officials said. The Army also plans to collect air and soil samples to assess exposure risks, according to the IDPH. The IEPA said it would watch data from its northern Illinois air monitoring network for signs of impacts on Illinois communities.
Pritzker and several members of Illinois’ congressional delegation wrote to the Army and the EPA on Thursday night expressing “grave concerns” about the plan.
“Alongside our neighbors in Iowa, we are also demanding answers about how this could affect people’s health and safety,” Pritzker said in a post sharing the letter.
This is a developing story.

Thousands of civilians in Iowa are in the path of an impending cloud of toxic chemicals to be unleashed when the US army detonates tons of aging explosives at a massive munitions factory on Monday.

sources.news_title: Army plans Iowa detonation this week despite court stay over toxic plumes
sources.text:
(Tribune News Service) — The Army still plans to detonate at an Iowa ammunition plant Monday or Tuesday, according to a Saturday court filing, a plan that was postponed last week by a court stay after public outcry over concerns that the explosion would likely release plumes of toxic lead dust into the air.
The Department of Justice, which filed the notice, said there is an “immediate risk” that the lead will explode on its own as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees this week, allowing the Army to invoke an exception and proceed with the controlled detonation without an emergency permit that environmental groups challenged last week.
“In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion,” the DOJ said, noting that it would allow the Army to minimize risk to the public, and that the agency “intends to act consistent with” the terms of the emergency permit even if it is not in effect.
Army officials have claimed they have no other choice than to blow up 68 drums containing 9,500 pounds of highly volatile, extremely hazardous lead azide at an ammunition depot in southeast Iowa.
According to reporting by The New York Times, the Army had hired a company to chemically neutralize the lead azide but canceled the contract two months later, citing safety concerns.
Initially, the Army’s computer modeling showed a plume of brain-damaging lead could have blown more than 100 miles into western Illinois on Friday, depending on weather conditions.
Environmental groups sued the Army on Thursday seeking to stop or delay the detonations, which could go on for at least four hours outside Middletown, Iowa, less than 8 miles west of the Mississippi River border between the state and Illinois.
“There is no safe level of lead in the body, and when inhaled or swallowed, it can pose serious health risks,” said Sameer Vohra, director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, in a news release last week.
A neurotoxin, lead is particularly harmful to children and pregnant women, and can cause developmental delays, difficulty learning and behavioral issues, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Lead azide has long been used as an explosive to trigger bombs and rockets, though it is being phased out by the armed forces because of concerns about its volatility and toxicity.
It remains unclear why the Army allowed stores of lead azide to degrade at its Iowa ammunition plant to the point that moving it off-site posed an “unacceptable risk of accidental detonation,” according to documents published on its website. According to The New York Times, the material stored at the facility had been considered stable for years until an inspection earlier this year revealed the presence of crystals that make it risky to even open the barrels it was stored in.
“Destroying it in place is the only responsible option,” Army officials state in the documents, one of which was only signed on Thursday. Doing so “restores vital military-industrial readiness,” they contend.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency granted an emergency permit for the detonations just last week. Documents posted online by the Army show the military branch has been consulting with the EPA for months about the plans, yet the public wasn’t notified until recently. Illinois EPA said it also had not been notified of the detonation by its federal counterpart.

sources.news_title: U.S. Army tells court it will go ahead with detonation in Iowa by Tuesday
Court pauses Iowa lead azide permit, but EPA says the Army may still detonate the material
sources.text:
Appeals Court Pauses Iowa Lead Azide Permit, but EPA Says the Army Could Still Detonate Without It
Developing Story Note: This report covers new developments involving the planned detonation of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. Information may change as the court, the EPA, and the Army act. Latest verified update: court filings reported by KWQC on Nov. 22, 2026.
A federal appeals court has temporarily blocked the EPA permit that would let the Army detonate about 5 tons of degraded lead azide stored in 68 drums at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The Eighth Circuit's one-sentence order stays the permit "until the emergency motion for stay is ruled upon by this court," CBS News Chicago reported.
The order came late last week, hours after Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle had already postponed the blast from Friday to Monday, Nov. 23, Fortune reported. In a Friday filing, government lawyers for the EPA argued that agency rules may let the Army treat the waste without a permit in a qualifying emergency.
For families in southeast Iowa and western Illinois, that leaves a weekend of uncertainty. The court has paused the permit, but it is not clear whether that stops the blast. The City of Fort Madison said it was told the detonation would happen Monday or Tuesday, KWQC reported on the court's deadline.
A Temporary Stay and a Sunday Deadline
The Iowa Environmental Council and the Iowa chapter of the Sierra Club asked the court to halt the permit, which the EPA issued Nov. 13. They argued that residents had extremely short notice and that the evidence the EPA relied on was not made public, according to CBS.
The court's order is an administrative stay, a short pause while judges consider the full emergency motion. It sets no end date. The court gave the EPA until noon Sunday, Nov. 22, to respond.
The EPA's Friday notice said the agency would oppose keeping the permit on hold and argued that the court order applies only to the permit. Government lawyers wrote that "in qualifying emergency situations," EPA regulations allow the Army to treat the waste without an EPA permit. The Army is not a party to the case.
Thien Chau, a senior attorney at Earthjustice, which represents the challengers, called that provision "an extraordinary and extreme backstop," Fortune reported. The Army had not said publicly whether it would proceed while the stay is in place.
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds activated the State Emergency Operations Center to coordinate state, federal and local agencies ahead of a possible blast.
Background on the Degraded Explosive
MedicalDaily previously reported that the Army delayed the blast to Monday, Nov. 23, citing public safety and the need to share information with state and local officials. Telle called Monday the "latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop," which he said could further destabilize the material.
The drums had been stored on site for more than 20 years in a mixture of ethanol and water. The Army says the material degraded and recrystallized, making it highly sensitive to friction and shock, and its environmental assessment says the problem was discovered in March 2026.
Army maps for the original Friday detonation projected dust settling across a stretch of roughly 25 miles north of the plant, with low levels of airborne lead possibly traveling farther, according to Fortune. Those maps are modeled projections, not measurements, and can change with the weather.
Lead Risks for Children and Pregnant Residents
Iowa health officials say no safe level of lead exposure has been identified. Lead is a neurotoxin, and young children face the greatest risk because they play on the ground and put their hands in their mouths, University of Iowa experts told Iowa Public Radio. Exposure during pregnancy is also a concern because lead can affect a developing baby.
Wind may dilute the dust, though it can also carry it farther. "That means it smears it out more," said Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a University of Iowa professor of occupational and environmental health. Settled lead can still remain on soil, sandboxes and play equipment.
Cleanup advice differs. Army spokesperson Justine Barati told Radio Iowa that residents worried about dust could "hose that off, and it's gone," according to Fortune. University of Iowa experts told Iowa Public Radio that rinsing washes lead into the dirt rather than removing it, and the challengers' court filings called the hose-off advice harmful misinformation.
Testing also costs money. Peter Thorne of the University of Iowa College of Public Health said people could get a follow-up blood lead test a few months later for reassurance, but noted that "many people might not be able to afford that."
Plans for Families While the Court Decides
Residents can plan for either outcome: a blast early in the week or a longer wait. Families near Middletown City Park and Butterfly Park were previously asked to leave for several hours around the blast because it could break windows, and residents needing shelter were invited to the Armed Forces Reserve Center, ABC News reported. Updated guidance has not been released.
If a blast proceeds, people who cannot leave the area were advised to stay indoors with windows and doors closed during the possible exposure period. After officials say that period has ended, residents were told to clean children's play surfaces and windowsills. Wet-wiping rather than dry-dusting, removing shoes at the door and washing children's hands after outdoor play can also limit swallowed dust.
The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services has posted a public health fact sheet on the detonation explaining how people can be exposed by breathing lead particles and through dust that settles on soil, vehicles and playgrounds. It says blood lead testing is the recommended way to evaluate possible exposure, so parents of young children and pregnant residents can ask a health care provider whether a test makes sense.
Several school districts, including the Burlington Community School District, had planned Friday closures and had not announced updated plans after the postponement.
The next step is the court's ruling on the emergency motion. MedicalDaily will report the decision, any detonation date and any air, soil or water results.
Key Questions Answered
What did the court do? The Eighth Circuit issued a temporary administrative stay of the EPA permit for the detonation.
Does the stay stop the blast? It is unclear. EPA lawyers argued that the Army may be able to act without a permit in a qualifying emergency.
When could the detonation happen? No date is confirmed. Fort Madison said it was told Monday or Tuesday.
Why does the Army want to detonate the lead azide? The material degraded and became highly sensitive to shock and friction, according to the Army and EPA.
Who faces the greatest risk? Young children and pregnant people, because lead can harm brain development.
What should families do if it proceeds? Stay indoors with windows and doors closed, then wet-clean surfaces and wash children's hands after outdoor play.

The Department of Justice, which filed the notice, said there is an “immediate risk” that the lead azide at the plant will explode on its own as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees this week, allowing the Army to invoke an exception and proceed with the controlled detonation without an emergency permit that environmental groups challenged last week.
Officials are urging nearby residents to take precautions such as staying indoors with doors and windows closed for 24 to 48 hours after detonation. No official starting time had been announced by Sunday evening.
Army officials have claimed they have no other choice than to blow up 68 drums containing 9,500 pounds of highly volatile, extremely hazardous lead azide at an ammunition depot in Middletown, a small city in southeast Iowa.
“In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion,” the DOJ said, noting that it would allow the Army to minimize risk to the public, and that the agency “intends to act consistent with” the terms of the emergency permit even if it is not in effect.
During a March inspection, a stockpile of lead azide was found to be degraded and crystallized. As outside temperatures drop, the Army says, the crystals can break more easily in freezing temperatures, risking a chain reaction that could cause an uncontrolled explosion and dispersal.
Additionally, the bunkers where the barrels are located are now more vulnerable to temperature changes, according to the DOJ filing, after the blast doors were removed ahead of the detonation and cannot be replaced.
Initially, the Army’s computer modeling showed a plume of brain-damaging lead could have blown more than 100 miles into western Illinois on Friday, depending on weather conditions. It had previously said it would provide map updates 48 hours, six hours and every hour thereafter before detonation. But the agency had not published updated models and maps of the plume’s path for the new detonation date as of Sunday evening. The Illinois Environmental Protection Agency has requested updated plume modeling as well.
“The wind patterns have shifted significantly, which means that potential community exposures have likely changed without visible effort by the Army to provide updated information to the public,” a news release from the Iowa Environmental Council said Sunday.
According to the National Weather Service in Quad Cities in Davenport, Iowa, which also covers southwestern and west central Illinois, winds will be coming from the northwest on Monday at about 10 to 20 mph, with some gusts between 15 and 20 mph, “with winds decreasing throughout the day,” said Ada Ellingworth, a meteorologist at the office.
“Generally, the very top end of that would be around what we would consider breezy,” she added. “With high pressure moving in, we’re expecting lighter winds that overnight will be (coming from) the north, and by Tuesday morning, being from the northeast, under five miles per hour.”
Army documents stated that the planned detonation Friday would be called off if winds exceeded 15 mph.
Illinois’ Hancock County is just south of Middletown, immediately across the state line. Dallas City, the county’s northernmost municipality, is a 27-mile drive. Mercer County is to the northeast, Henderson County to the east and McDonough County to the southeast.
U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen, whose district is located in central and northwestern Illinois and includes parts of Mercer and McDonough, is a trained meteorologist. He said that if the barrels were detonated last Friday, with such a strong southerly wind — blowing from the south toward the north — the toxic dust would have spread over much of eastern Iowa.
“Now, on Monday or Tuesday, there’s a lighter northerly wind, but a new trajectory places western Illinois downwind and at risk,” he said in a video shared to social media. “As a reminder, wind direction tells us the direction; wind speed tells us how fast anything would travel. So nothing is instant, and not everyone’s impacted. Know that.”
Environmental groups sued the Army on Thursday seeking to stop or delay the detonations, which could go on for at least four hours outside, less than 8 miles west of the Mississippi River border between Iowa and Illinois.
“There is no safe level of lead in the body, and when inhaled or swallowed, it can pose serious health risks,” said Sameer Vohra, director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, in a news release last week.
A neurotoxin, lead is particularly harmful to children and pregnant women. It can cause developmental delays, difficulty learning and behavioral issues, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. There are also concerns that the dust will settle on agricultural soil and pollute waterways like the Mississippi.
The Army is coordinating with farmers regarding harvest timing; cleanup, if required, could temporarily suspend certain leases. It will be responsible for cleaning up soil if it is sampled and exceeds regulatory thresholds for lead. According to the agency, it will also monitor air quality for airborne lead dust. Last week, Illinois officials said no information on the breadth of said monitoring had been shared.
Lead azide has long been used as an explosive to trigger bombs and rockets, though it is being phased out by the armed forces because of concerns about its volatility and toxicity.
It remains unclear why the Army allowed stores of lead azide to degrade at its Iowa ammunition plant to the point that moving it off-site posed an “unacceptable risk of accidental detonation,” according to documents published on its website.
“As a meteorologist, I want to know why so much time has passed with those optimal weather days until the cold weather determined that we are out of options,” Sorensen said.
According to The New York Times, the material stored at the facility had been considered stable for years until an inspection earlier this year revealed the presence of crystals that make it risky to even open the barrels it was stored in.
“The new information from the DOJ indicates that the problem is significantly worse than the Army originally shared,” said Michael Schmidt, general counsel for the environmental council. “It appears that detonation may be, at this point, the only feasible option due to how long this problem was allowed to persist.”
According to reporting by The New York Times, the Army had hired a company to chemically neutralize the lead azide but canceled the contract two months later, citing “unacceptable risk to human safety.” The process would have required significantly more physical manipulation of the drums by personnel over a prolonged period of seven to 22 days, “drastically increasing the probability of accidental, fatal detonation during handling,” according to an environmental assessment by the Army.
On Sunday morning, the environment council, alongside Sierra Club and Earthjustice, filed declarations with the court calling out the Army’s “inadequate” public notice and information, and questioning the federal government’s claims that other, safer alternatives were considered.
“Destroying it in place is the only responsible option,” Army officials had stated in documents, one of which was only signed on Thursday. Doing so “restores vital military-industrial readiness,” they contend.
The U.S. EPA granted an emergency permit for the detonations Nov. 13. Documents posted online by the Army show the military branch has been consulting with the EPA for months about the plans, yet the public wasn’t notified until recently. Illinois EPA said it also had not been notified of the detonation by its federal counterpart.
Chicago Tribune’s Michael Hawthorne contributed.

sources.news_title: Trump Administration Confirms Plans to Detonate Iowa Lead Without a Permit
sources.text:
The Trump administration said it intends to detonate lead explosives in Iowa this week despite a court order temporarily blocking it, pointing to the risk of an uncontrolled explosion in cold weather that makes it too dangerous to wait.
In court filings Saturday, Justice Department attorneys laid out why the Army plans to use emergency authority granted by the Environmental Protection Agency to move forward without a permit, and an Army official for the first time described in greater detail how the situation became so dangerous.
The 68 barrels of degrading lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant are crystallizing, and the crystals are more likely to break in cold temperatures, setting off an explosive chain reaction that could “cause an uncontrolled dispersal of lead azide into the environment,” the DOJ filing says. Temperatures are forecast to drop below freezing Sunday night and then into the low twenties Monday and Tuesday night.
And the Army said its preparations to detonate the explosives have made the situation even more dangerous and cannot be reversed, since heavy metal blast doors were removed and replaced with temporary plywood insulated with foam.
Trending
“The bunkers, where the barrels are located, are now more vulnerable to temperature changes because the blast doors were removed in preparation of the controlled detonation and cannot be replaced,” the DOJ filing says.
The Army has been under intense pressure from Iowa and Illinois leaders and from environmental groups, all urging the Defense Department to delay its plan to deliberately destroy the lead azide in an effort to avoid an uncontrolled explosion from the volatile substance. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds said she was not notified of the Army’s plan until Monday, when it first published maps that showed the possibility of a toxic lead dust plume stretching over parts of Iowa and into Illinois.
Environmental groups filed a lawsuit Thursday intended to delay the explosion, and on Friday the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily blocked the EPA’s emergency permit. The detonation is currently scheduled to take place Monday.
The Trump administration’s legal response Saturday confirms that the Army intends to blow up the explosives without a permit even if the court decides to continue blocking it, exercising emergency authority granted by the EPA.
In the event of an uncontrolled detonation, the filing describes the dangerous scenarios envisioned by Army experts. An uncontrolled explosion could send lead into the air over unprepared surrounding communities, causing public panic. Some of the lead azide could be jettisoned into other parts of the ammunition plant, undetonated in the initial reaction, necessitating secondary explosions in areas also unprepared for such work.
“Unfavorable winds could increase the dispersion of lead dust into the community,” the DOJ filing said. “An uncontrolled deportation of nearly five tons of primary explosive would endanger soldiers, contractors, and the surrounding communities, all without many of the protective measures meant to minimize the risks from the blast — harm that cannot be undone.”
An Army official, Aaron Teller, in a court declaration, said the Army found that 58 of the 68 barrels have crystallization present around their lids during a late April inspection, meaning the lids of the barrels aren’t safe to remove. The Army first discovered there was a problem with the barrels in March, during a routine inspection, and then prohibited Army personnel from accessing the barrels at that point onward, according to EPA permitting documents obtained by The Washington Sun.
A contractor — American Ordnance — is usually in charge of opening the barrel lids every September to refill the liquid that historically has covered the lead azide and is used to prevent crystallization. But this year, the contractor has not refilled the liquid because of the safety issues, increasing the risks, Teller said in the declaration.
The Army has been preparing mitigation measures for more than a month, building barriers around the site where the lead azide is stored and planning to soak the area ahead of and after the explosion to limit lead dust dispersion.
The environmental groups challenging the Army’s plan also filed a declaration Sunday from explosives and EPA experts, who said that they believed the Army’s mitigation measures would have significantly reduced the risk of explosion from quickly falling temperatures.
“Based on my training and experience, the storage conditions described in EPA’s permit, and historical and forecast weather for the Burlington area, it is my opinion that the forecast weather does not support the Army’s position that the detonation must occur no later than November 23, 2026,” wrote Mark J. Thomas, a retired EPA official from Region 7, the area that oversees the ammunition plant.
The Army reviewed the possibility of using chemicals to destroy the lead azide instead of blowing it up, but doing so would have required opening the lids of the barrels, which experts deemed too dangerous and risked causing unintentional explosions, according to an early September letter from Army officials to the EPA. On May 8, then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll determined that intentionally detonating the lead was the safest approach, according to the letter.
The Army hired a contractor in April to explore that chemical approach but then canceled the contract two months later for safety reasons, according to The New York Times. The contract was worth $30,000 and cancelled on May 27, according to federal government contracting records reviewed by The Sun.
Correction: A previous version of this story incorrectly reported which Army official filed a court declaration.

sources.news_title: Iowa detonation of lead will proceed under emergency powers, Army says, bypassing court order
sources.text:
By Jack Queen
NEW YORK, Nov 22 (Reuters) – The US Army will detonate 68 barrels of toxic lead azide in Iowa by Tuesday under emergency legal powers that allow it to bypass a court order blocking the controversial plan, the Trump administration told a court this weekend.
“The Army must perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion, and the Army intends to act by November 24, 2026,” the Justice Department said in a court filing late on Saturday.
The US Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit temporarily halted the detonation by freezing the Army’s environmental permit on Thursday after environmental groups sued to halt the operation. The government said in Saturday night’s filing that the Army plans to move forward without a permit by invoking an emergency munitions and explosives exception to federal environmental protection laws.
Federal officials say the detonation must go forward within the next several days because a drop in temperatures could destabilize the material and cause an uncontrolled explosion.
The Army previously postponed plans to detonate the degraded lead azide, an explosive used in military munitions, after public outcry by residents and farmers near Middletown, Iowa.
The Army did not immediately respond to an inquiry on Sunday about the precise timing of the detonation.
The Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club’s Iowa chapter filed the lawsuit. Earthjustice, a nonprofit environmental law organization suing on behalf of the groups, did not immediately respond to an email on Sunday seeking comment.
The plaintiffs have argued that the detonations would release a toxic plume of lead dust into the air that could travel 100 miles (161 kilometers) north of the site, depending on weather conditions.
In a statement on Thursday, acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the Army had determined with the US Environmental Protection Agency that a controlled detonation to dispose of the degraded lead was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public.
Lead exposure can cause serious health problems, particularly in children, including damage to the brain and nervous system.
The Army has advised people to avoid the affected area during the detonation and urged anyone who could not leave beforehand to stay indoors, close windows and doors and shut off heating and cooling systems. Residents should wet-clean surfaces children may touch to remove any lead dust once the exposure period has ended, the Army said.
The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship has recommended that cattle farmers near the detonation site move their livestock, feed and equipment to alternate locations or indoors.
(Reporting by Jack Queen in New York; Editing by Sergio Non and Bill Berkrot)
