sources.news_title: Army tells court IAAAP detonation to happen by Tuesday without EPA permit
sources.text:
The Army has told a federal court they intend to detonate the nearly 10,000 pounds of unstable lead azide being stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown by Tuesday without the EPA permit being held up in a federal lawsuit.
The filing states that cooling temperatures in the coming days could cause the lead azide to explode and that the controlled detonation has been deemed necessary to prevent a surprise uncontrolled explosion.
On Thursday, acting Army Secretary Adam Telle announced on X (formerly known as Twitter) that the detonation was being postponed until Monday.
Telle did not say what time the detonation would occur, but said Monday was the "latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material."
Also on Thursday, the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ordered an administrative stay on the emergency permit granted to the Army by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), which temporarily suspended the permit, which the Army is legally required to have to carry out the detonation.
The emergency stay came following a lawsuit filed by Earthjustice on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Iowa Chapter of the Sierra Club.
In that lawsuit, those environmental groups alleged the EPA had not adequately considered the possible health and environmental risks posed by the detonation and argued that "less dangerous alternatives" have not properly been considered.
The lawsuit asked the court to issue a ruling on the EPA permit or issue an administrative stay to temporarily suspend the permit until the court can issue their ruling, which the court did on Thursday, giving the government a Sunday deadline to file their response.
In addition to arguing the Army did not need the EPA permit to conduct the detonation, the government also wrote the Army is legally able to carry out the detonation because the Army is responding to an emergency.
"The Government notifies the Court that the Department of the Army ('Army') intends to invoke the emergency munitions and explosives exclusion to EPA’s regulatory and permitting Resource Conservation and Recovery Act ('RCRA') requirements, under which the Army may perform treatment by controlled detonation of the lead azide waste without the Emergency Permit that is challenged in this petition," the filing states.
"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (the “Facility”) will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit in the next several days.
"The Army must perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion, and the Army intends to act by November 24, 2026.
"A controlled detonation allows the Army to implement measures to minimize the risk to the public, including the risk from the ejection of partial unexploded ordnances that can explode later from the Facility.
"The Army intends to act consistent with the terms of the Emergency Permit and its mitigation measures even if not in effect. That includes mitigation measures to minimize the risk of the dispersal of lead dust. In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion.
"The emergency exception does not depend on the Emergency Permit and is therefore not affected by, nor contradictory to, the terms of this Court’s administrative stay."
The government's response said there is "an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Facility will spontaneously explode," adding that the "barrels holding the waste cannot be removed due to the risk of explosion, which prevents the Army from taking other measures to reduce that risk."
As outside temperatures continue to drop, the government says the risk for an uncontrolled explosion has increased because of crystals that have formed inside the barrels storing the lead azide could break more easily in freezing temperatures, which could cause a chain reaction detonation that "could cause an uncontrolled dispersal of lead azide into the environment."
"Temperatures have already dropped below 30 degrees Fahrenheit, with temperature swings as low as 24 degrees and high as 70 degrees," the government wrote in the filing.
"These recent temperature swings have dramatically increased the risk of an uncontrolled explosion and threat to public safety.
"Further, the bunkers, where the barrels are located, are now more vulnerable to temperature changes because the blast doors were removed in preparation of the controlled detonation and cannot be replaced."
Under those circumstances, the government wrote that the EPA's RCRA regulations "provide an exemption from both substantive and permitting requirements to allow immediate action."
"A controlled detonation minimizes the risk associated with the resulting explosion," the government wrote.
"During a controlled detonation, the Army can implement a full suite of mitigation efforts including, providing advance public notice; performing the detonation under favorable weather conditions (e.g., less wind, light rain) to mitigate the spread of lead dust; wetting to reduce lead dust dispersal; treating the lead to prevent only a partial detonation; facilitating any necessary community evacuation; and monitoring to identify where any lead dust may spread and where any environmental response actions may be needed.
"Indeed, in preparation for the controlled detonation, the Army has already constructed protective barriers around the munitions bunkers to minimize the escape of blast material.
"A spontaneous explosion, on the other hand, is much riskier.
'In an uncontrolled explosion, the Army cannot implement its robust mitigation efforts.
"Failing to treat all the lead azide, for example, could result in a random dispersal of explosive material.
"This partially exploded lead azide could explode later —a second spontaneous explosion—creating extremely unsafe conditions for the public and for personnel conducting post-detonation cleanup. Unfavorable winds could increase the dispersion of lead dust in the community.
"And without public notice, the public may panic upon the spontaneous explosion.
"A controlled detonation is unquestionably much more protective to the public than an uncontrolled explosion.
"A controlled detonation is necessary now to respond to the immediate threat of an uncontrolled explosion of military munitions at the Facility. EPA’s regulations allow the Army’s planned action without the need for a permit and the Army intends to act on November 24, 2026...
"An uncontrolled detonation of nearly five tons of primary explosive would endanger soldiers, contractors, and the surrounding communities, all without many of the protective measures meant to minimize the risks from the blast—harm that cannot be undone.
"The environmental and health interests Petitioners seek to protect plainly are better served by a controlled detonation than by an uncontrolled explosion, which would not allow for wetting the blast material, control the timing to align with favorable weather conditions, and prior public notification, and could scatter partially destroyed lead azide.
"The real choice, in other words, is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned and mitigated detonation and an unplanned and unmitigated explosion.
"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action. Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."
The filing did not state what if the Army intends to conduct the detonation on Monday or Tuesday or what time it may occur.
As of 10 a.m. Sunday, the Army has not issued any further updates and it is unknown at this time which day or time they intend to carry out the detonation.
Check back for further updates as they become available.

US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
- Published
The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.
"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."
The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.
The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.
In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.
"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.
It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".
The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.
Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place.
Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.
On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible.
Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.
The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".
One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen.
"There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement.
The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, which filed the lawsuit on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause, filed a new motion on Sunday in response to the army's filing.
The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.
The motion includes declarations from environmental experts and local officials who support pausing the detonation, citing a lack of public notice and questioning the Army's claim that delay would cause significant risks.

The Army originally scheduled two controlled explosions for Friday. The Army then delayed them until Monday before the court stepped in.

The military said on Friday it was working closely with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the controlled explosion would be conducted in the safest manner possible.

"A controlled detonation allows the Army to implement measures to minimize the risk to the public, including the risk from the ejection of partial unexploded ordnances that can explode later from the Facility," the court filing says. "The Army intends to act consistent with the terms of the Emergency Permit and its mitigation measures even if not in effect. That includes mitigation measures to minimize the risk of the dispersal of lead dust. In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion."
In response to the Army's filing, the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club filed a motion Sunday seeking to supplement their emergency request to block the planned detonation.

In a statement Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club and Earthjustice questioned claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration, saying "this emergency is of the Army's own making."
"The Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public's demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm," said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau.
Iowa's new Democratic Senator-elect Josh Turek said in a statement Sunday that he is "concerned about the potential health risks resulting from the U.S. Army's planned detonation in Middletown and the lack of clear communication and transparency from the U.S. Army," and that he was "pushing for answers, including specifics of when the detonation is taking place."
"I also believe we need a full investigation into why this stockpile of lead azide, which has been at IAAAP for decades, was allowed to degrade into this critical state, why safer methods of disposal were not pursued, what other potentially dangerous materials are being stored at the IAAAP and their condition, and what procedures are needed to ensure this never happens again," he said. "The public also deserves answers as to why the U.S. Army's communication — both with the public and with Iowa officials — was delayed and inadequate from the beginning."
In March of this year, the Army said it discovered that 68 drums of lead azide at the site had started "recrystallization." The lead was stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a munitions plant built in 1941, which produces quality medium- and large-caliber munitions.

US Army says it must detonate explosives in Iowa due to coming cold weather
CHICAGO - The U.S. Army said it plans to conduct a detonation of old, unstable explosives at an ammunition plant in Iowa by Tuesday, despite health and environmental concerns by locals.
What we know:
In a court filing on Saturday, the Army said it must perform the detonation to "protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion."
Adding that the Army intends to "act" by Nov. 24, it explained that this is because there is a risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant could explode when temperatures drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit "in the next several days."
The Army said it would originally set off two controlled blasts and destroy the bomb-making chemicals on Friday, Nov. 20, but that was postponed after an uproar from local residents and officials.
According to the filing, the temperature swings have also "dramatically increased the risk of an uncontrolled explosion and threat to public safety."
Legal fight over detonation
The backstory:
Environmental groups filed a lawsuit in federal court to try to stop the explosion.
The planning process for the detonation began as officials found 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a small town of about 320 people just west of Burlington and the Mississippi River.
Routine inspections found that this specific batch had degraded to the point where normal handling was no longer safe.
Lead azide is sensitive to temperature changes. As a result, the Army decided to delay the detonation "until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material," Acting Army Sec. Adam Telle wrote on X.
While public health officials have expressed concerns, the Army has said the operation will have "no significant impact" on the surrounding environment. Crews plan to stack two-story sand barriers around the blast site, wet the soil and spray water to trap dust and contain debris.
What is lead azide?
Dig deeper:
Lead azide is a chemical compound used to ignite military ammunition. Since it's not being used, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency describes it as "hazardous waste."
Over time, old lead azide breaks down and becomes sensitive to friction and shock.
"This means that even a small quantity of lead azide can detonate with friction or heat, making it inherently dangerous to transport," Matthew McConnell, an assistant professor of chemistry at Western Illinois University, told FOX TV Stations.
Because loading it onto a truck and hauling it elsewhere is too risky, the Army obtained an emergency permit from the EPA on Nov. 13 to destroy it at the plant.

sources.news_title: Army plans to detonate degrading lead azide waste at Iowa plant on Tuesday, filings show
sources.text:
MIDDLETOWN, Iowa — The U.S. Army plans to detonate lead azide waste in Middletown on Tuesday, after a judge issued a stay to delay the detonation days ago.
In federal court records filed Saturday night, the Army indicated its intention to destroy the degrading waste at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant by November 24.
"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant ... will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit in the next several days," the filing reads.
"The Army must perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion ... a controlled detonation allows the Army to implement measures to minimize the risk to the public, including the risk from the ejection of partial unexploded ordnances that can explode later from the Facility," the filing reads.
The stay came at the request of environmental groups including the Iowa Environmental Council, the Sierra Club, and Earth Justice. The groups released a statement Sunday that reads, in part:
Early Sunday morning, the groups filed declarations with the court that call out the Army’s inadequate public notice and information and question the Army’s and EPA’s claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration.
The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a statement with the court late on Saturday, Nov. 21, indicating that the Army intends to invoke emergency provisions of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) to detonate 9,773.5 pounds of lead azide stored at the Iowa Army Ammunitions Plant without a permit from the EPA. According to the DOJ’s statement, the Army intends to do so no later than Nov. 24.
This emergency is of the Army’s own making. The Army has not publicly provided details about why the lead azide was not disposed of before it became so dangerous.
The Army’s own storage and inspection practices allowed a primary explosive to sit until it reportedly degraded to the point that any alternative disposal method is now deemed too dangerous. The lack of transparency raises real questions about the scope and extent of potential impacts.
Governor Kim Reynolds shared on Sunday a A dedicated website for Iowans seeking more information about the planned detonation.
“While the detonation is a federal operation, it’s important for the state to be engaged in the preparation process so we can support the work of our federal partners in responding to the needs of Iowans,” said Governor Reynolds. “Protecting the health and safety of our people and communities is our highest priority.”

Court stay prevents US Army from detonating bomb-making chemicals in Iowa
An inspection earlier this year at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant determined that the lead azide, which is used in munitions production, had started to degrade. The crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the Army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan.
According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums' contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation.
The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their petition that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Court records: U.S. Army plans to carry out lead azide detonation after federal court pause
sources.text:
U.S. Army plans to carry out lead azide detonation at Iowa plant 'by Tuesday,' court records say
Environmental organizations are responding just hours after court records revealed the U.S. Army plans to detonate lead azide waste in Middletown, Iowa, by Tuesday, despite a pause on the permit to do so.
On Sunday evening, Washington County Emergency Management confirmed to Des Moines sister station KCCI that the detonation will move forward on Tuesday, however, an exact time was not noted.
According to court documents submitted early Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club are asking the Eighth Circuit Court to accept additional evidence in their request to pause the detonation.
Originally, the Army planned to detonate several tons of the bomb-making chemicals on Friday, but after public concern, the plans were pushed to Monday. Army officials say the chemicals have degraded, making them too dangerous to move.
The additional evidence includes a statement from Mark J. Thomas, a former EPA air-monitoring official, disputing the Army's claim that the lead azide should be detonated by Tuesday due to a change in the weather.
His statement says that because the drums containing the lead azide are stored in a semi-underground structure, a temperature drop of approximately 20 degrees would not affect the temperature of the drums and would not increase the hazard.
The new filings also contain a statement from Ranajit Sahu, a consultant with decades of experience in environmental, mechanical and chemical engineering. His statement questions whether the proposed blast controls are enough to protect human health.
In a statement shared with sister station KCCI, the Iowa Environmental Council, Earthjustice and the Sierra Club say this new filing is a response to the Army's announcement that it plans to detonate the lead azide even while the permit has been paused.
"This emergency is of the Army’s own making. The Army has not publicly provided details about why the lead azide was not disposed of before it became so dangerous," the statement read in part. "The Army’s own storage and inspection practices allowed a primary explosive to sit until it reportedly degraded to the point that any alternative disposal method is now deemed too dangerous. The lack of transparency raises real questions about the scope and extent of potential impacts."
KCCI reached out to the U.S. Army for more information but did not immediately hear back.
Previous coverage
Federal court records filed late Saturday say the Department of the Army plans to detonate the lead azide waste in Middletown, Iowa, on or by Tuesday, Nov. 24.
On Thursday, a federal appeals court paused the Environmental Protection Agency's permit that would allow the U.S. Army to detonate several tons of lead waste.

In Saturday's court filing, the government said it plans to use an emergency munitions and explosives exclusion to the EPA's permit. The government argues it needs to perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion.
The Army has said the expected temperature drops early this week could trigger an uncontrolled explosion. The filing also warns an uncontrolled blast could scatter explosive material that might detonate later.
The government says the lead azide has deteriorated and that crystals in the waste could break as temperatures drop. The government also says other options would require handling the material in ways that could also trigger an uncontrolled explosion.
The Army still plans to use the mitigation measures laid out in the special permit, even though it is on pause.
That explosion was originally set for Friday, then moved to Monday.
The petition challenging the EPA permit was brought by the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club.
Several lines of the filing say the Army plans to detonate the lead azide "by" Nov. 24. One paragraph says the Army plans to act "on" Nov. 24. We've reached out for clarification.

sources.news_title: The Army plans to blow up tons of toxic explosives. It rejected a safer option.
sources.text:
The Army plans to blow up tons of toxic explosives. It rejected a safer option.
|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
In March, when the Army discovered nearly 5 tons of rapidly deteriorating explosives at an Iowa base, it faced two main choices: hire a company to safely dissolve the chemicals, or blow them up.
The Army awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based firm that uses chemicals to neutralize munitions. But it canceled the deal two months later, citing safety concerns, opting to blow up nearly 5 tons of the material instead.
The detonation is scheduled for Monday. Residents, environmentalists and elected leaders are in an uproar because the material contains lead, and the blast could potentially contaminate hundreds of square miles with toxic dust.
The Army did not respond to questions about its canceled deal with MuniRem and why it chose to blow up the dangerous material. The details about the MuniRem contract have not previously been reported.
It is unclear why the Army did not remove and dispose of the drums of lead azide before they reached the point of deterioration that forced the decision to detonate them.
There is no safe level of exposure to lead, which is a neurotoxin. It is particularly dangerous to children and pregnant women. It can interfere with fetal brain development, cause cognitive and behavioral harm and increase the risk of premature births or miscarriage.
Earlier in the past week, the Army stated in documents clearing the way for Monday’s planned detonation that chemical alternatives “offered environmental protections by avoiding a blast plume.” The documents didn’t name the alternative method, but said it could process as much as 10 drums per day, requiring up to 22 days to get through the stockpile in Iowa.
The documents also said that the alternative had been “eliminated from detailed study” because it required personnel to handle the explosives and would drastically increase the probability of an accidental detonation, creating an “unacceptable risk to human safety.”
In a letter Friday to Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, the Environmental Protection Agency said that those concerns had been raised by the Army, Federal Bureau of Investigation, and Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.
The agencies said that any movement of the barrels, or even removing the lids, could cause a spontaneous detonation, posing “a significant risk to personnel and the surrounding population,” EPA regional administrator Jim Macy wrote. None of the agencies immediately responded to requests for comment.
That came after the acting secretary of the Army, Adam Telle, said in a statement on Thursday that there was urgency to destroy the lead azide because temperatures were expected to drop below freezing, which could “risk further destabilization” of the material.
An environmental group is challenging the detonation permit granted to the Army by the Environmental Protection Agency. The Justice Department argued on Friday that the Army has the authority to blow up the cache, regardless of an EPA permit. A federal court has yet to rule on the complaint.
While detonation of unneeded or unstable ordnance in the open air has for decades been a standard disposal method, in more recent years businesses have developed chemical processes that can break apart explosives at the molecular level. The resulting byproducts are typically nonhazardous and can be buried in landfills.
But such chemical sprays are relatively new and unfamiliar to many in the military who have spent their careers blowing up unneeded or unstable munitions on demolition ranges.
MuniRem presented its chemical technology in March to an expert panel assembled by the Army to find a solution to the lead azide crisis at the Iowa ammunition facility.
Lead azide is sensitive to heat, shock and friction, meaning it can easily detonate if mishandled. And when it degrades, these risks increase.
MuniRem’s technology uses a sulfur-based solution that breaks down explosives and immobilizes toxic chemicals, rather than detonating or burning them.
According to materials presented to the expert panel by MuniRem, and reviewed by The New York Times, the company presented case studies in which its solution was applied to unstable lead azide, including the disposal of 412 pounds of aged lead azide that had been poorly stored inside an ammunition bunker.
In an interview, Valentine Nzengung, MuniRem’s CEO and a professor in environmental geochemistry at the University of Georgia, said that MuniRem had proposed spraying the bunker interiors and barrel surfaces to neutralize risks of spontaneous explosions. That would make it possible to determine how to safely open the barrels and neutralize the lead azide inside, he said.
“Our position on this is very straightforward,” he said. “We believe that any disposal decision should protect public health.”
Following the presentation, MuniRem was hired in late March to dispose of the volatile explosive. But two months later, the Army terminated the contract.
Nzengung said the Army gave no reason for the cancellation aside from the fact that then-Secretary of the Army, Dan Driscoll, had made the final determination to order the controlled detonation instead. That involves placing explosive charges around the material in both bunkers and blowing them up simultaneously, destroying the lead azide in the process.
According to emails reviewed by the Times, an Army contracting officer told the company that the decision not to use MuniRem’s chemical neutralization method “was not based on deficiencies” in MuniRem’s proposed technical approach.
Nzengung of MuniRem said the company has filed public records requests seeking more information on why its technology was dismissed, and has not received a response.
Driscoll resigned as Army secretary on Aug. 31, after clashing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over Hegseth’s removal of qualified Army officers from promotion lists without explanation.
In a statement provided to the Times, a spokesperson for Driscoll said when he was in office and became aware of the lead azide problem at the Iowa plant, he commissioned a study with several federal agencies that oversee explosive safety matters and agreed with their findings that controlled detonation offered the safest possible solution, though Driscoll believed that more work needed to be done to notify state and local authorities ahead of time to coordinate a public response.
Alternatives to open-air detonation have been gaining acceptance. In 2019, the National Academies of Sciences reviewed MuniRem’s process, along with thermal and chemical alternatives to open burning or detonation, and found that it “can be conducted indoors with little danger to the user or community.”
The Academies also listed shortcomings of the chemical process, namely that it could be slow. Still, the method “has been demonstrated and validated on several field scale projects,” it noted. Workers could wear personal protective gear “to ensure no contact with the reactive chemicals when spraying the MuniRem solution,” it said.
A January 2025 EPA guide to detonation alternatives also lists chemical neutralization, including MuniRem, as a valid treatment technology for lead azide.
Andrew J. Whelton, a professor of environmental chemistry and engineering at Purdue University, said any risk of fatality was a valid concern and should drive decision-making. Still, “if there was a non-detonation option that could have been chosen and the deliberate detonation could be avoided, then this is a major decision,” he said. “Open burning, open detonation is a practice that is used as a last resort.”
The Iowa base plays a critical role in the nation’s defense as the main facility for loading explosives into artillery and mortar shells used by the Pentagon. According to an internal Army history report, the site was built from 1940 to 1941 as part of the massive mobilization for arms during World War II and sits on 19,000 acres.
Deakin Donley, a retired Navy explosive ordnance disposal technician said the rapidly-approaching temperature shift meant there would likely not be a reasonable way to stabilize such a large stockpile. “Proceeding with detonation is the only viable option now, unfortunately,” he said.
This incident would be “a lesson learned for industry and stockpile management,” he added. “Ensuring routine inspections and maintenance would have likely prevented this, and it will be an example cited for decades to come.”

sources.text:
Army says it can detonate lead azide at Iowa plant despite court pause, new DOJ filing
MIDDLETOWN, Iowa — The U.S. Army says it plans to detonate degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant by Tuesday, arguing it can act under a federal emergency rule even though an appeals court has temporarily stayed the Environmental Protection Agency permit for the operation.
The Justice Department filed a notice Saturday with the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals saying the Army intends to use an emergency exclusion in federal hazardous-waste regulations to conduct a controlled detonation without the permit. The filing says the Army plans to act by Nov. 24 to address what it describes as an immediate risk of an uncontrolled explosion.
The notice argues the court’s administrative stay applies to the EPA permit but does not bar the Army from acting under a separate emergency authority. The court has not authorized a detonation under that authority in the filing provided.
The Army says the material has deteriorated and become sensitive to friction, and that moving the barrels could trigger an explosion. It says falling temperatures could increase the risk of an uncontrolled blast. The Army plans to use mitigation measures during a controlled detonation, including wetting material to limit lead dust, monitoring for contamination and providing public notice, according to the filing.
The dispute stems from a lawsuit filed by the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club’s Iowa chapter. The groups are challenging the EPA’s emergency permit and say the Army did not provide enough public notice or adequately consider safer disposal methods. They have warned that lead dust from the operation could affect communities far from the plant, depending on weather.
The Army released new filings on Sunday stating that "this Court should reject Petitioners’ attempt to include three new declarations that seek to address the scientific and technical merits of EPA’s permit decision and to present expert testimony."
The army also released their opposition to the emergency motion for stay, stating "Army munitions safety experts determined that controlled detonation is the only safe way to treat the waste, because every alternative requires disturbing material that may explode if disturbed."
The filings also state "The choice therefore is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned detonation (timed for favorable weather, preceded by public notice, and followed by monitoring and cleanup) and an unplanned explosion that could come at any moment, with no warning and no safeguards"
The Army had initially planned the detonation for Friday, then postponed it to Monday. The court’s stay put the permit on hold while it considers the groups’ challenge.

In a statement shared with KCCI, the Iowa Environmental Council, Earthjustice and the Sierra Club say this new filing is a response to the Army's announcement that it plans to detonate the lead azide even while the permit has been paused.
"This emergency is of the Army’s own making. The Army has not publicly provided details about why the lead azide was not disposed of before it became so dangerous," the statement read in part. "The Army’s own storage and inspection practices allowed a primary explosive to sit until it reportedly degraded to the point that any alternative disposal method is now deemed too dangerous. The lack of transparency raises real questions about the scope and extent of potential impacts."
KCCI reached out to the U.S. Army for more information but did not immediately hear back.
Previous coverage
Federal court records filed late Saturday say the Department of the Army plans to detonate the lead azide waste in Middletown, Iowa, on or by Tuesday, Nov. 24.
On Thursday, a federal appeals court paused the Environmental Protection Agency's permit that would allow the U.S. Army to detonate several tons of lead waste.
WATCH ABOVE: Iowans share concerns about lead azide as court ruling pauses detonation
In Saturday's court filing, the government said it plans to use an emergency munitions and explosives exclusion to the EPA's permit. The government argues it needs to perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion.
The Army has said the expected temperature drops early this week could trigger an uncontrolled explosion. The filing also warns an uncontrolled blast could scatter explosive material that might detonate later.
The government says the lead azide has deteriorated and that crystals in the waste could break as temperatures drop. The government also says other options would require handling the material in ways that could also trigger an uncontrolled explosion.
The Army still plans to use the mitigation measures laid out in the special permit, even though it is on pause.
That explosion was originally set for Friday, then moved to Monday.
The petition challenging the EPA permit was brought by the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club.
Several lines of the filing say the Army plans to detonate the lead azide "by" Nov. 24. One paragraph says the Army plans to act "on" Nov. 24. We've reached out for clarification.

UPDATE: Army says it will proceed with lead azide detonation
MIDDLETOWN, Iowa (KCRG) - The U.S. Army said it plans to carry out a controlled detonation of nearly five tons of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant by November 24, warning that dropping temperatures have created an “immediate threat” of an uncontrolled blast.
It’s unclear exactly what day and what time the detonation will happen.
In a federal court filing Saturday, lawyers for the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) notified judges that the Army intends to invoke an emergency exemption in federal hazardous waste rules to destroy lead azide stored at the plant in Middletown, Iowa.
With temperatures set to dip below 30 degrees this week, Army officials said the changing weather conditions have increased the risk that the lead azide could “spontaneously explode.”
The Army said the bunker where the lead azide is located is now more vulnerable to temperature changes because the blast doors were removed in preparation for the controlled detonation and cannot be replaced.
The lawsuit from The Iowa Environmental Council and the Iowa chapter of the Sierra Club challenged an emergency permit the EPA granted to the U.S. Army for the detonation.
The groups allege in their lawsuit that many Iowans did not receive information about potential lead exposure.
The U.S. Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals ordered an administrative stay Thursday, blocking the EPA permit that allowed the Army to conduct the controlled detonation of lead azide.
In a post on Facebook Saturday, the City of Fort Madison said it had been notified that the detonation will take place either Monday or Tuesday.

sources.news_title: Court Halts Army Plan to Detonate Toxic Lead Amid Legal Challenges
sources.text:
Court Halts Army Plan to Detonate Toxic Lead Amid Legal Challenges
The U.S. Army planned to dispose of nearly five tons of unstable, lead-based explosives at an Iowa ammunition plant by blowing them up and telling nearby residents to stay indoors. The explosions threatened to scatter toxic lead particles across surrounding communities and farmland. Now, a federal appeals court has halted the plan following a legal challenge by environmental groups questioning both its safety and legality.
The Order
On Thursday, the Eighth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily suspended an Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) permit authorizing two explosions at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.
The court’s one-sentence order stated, in full:
An administrative stay of the emergency permit issued by the Environmental Protection Agency is granted until the emergency motion for stay is ruled upon by this court.
The order followed a petition and emergency motion filed that day by the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club, represented by Earthjustice. Both filings belong to one case.
It is an administrative pause, not a decision that the EPA acted illegally. The judges have yet to resolve the groups’ request for a longer stay or the underlying challenge to the permit.
The Army had already moved Friday’s detonation to Monday, November 23. The court’s intervention left even that revised date uncertain.
Twenty Years in Storage
The dispute concerns 68 drums containing roughly 9,700 pounds of lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive used in military ammunition.
According to the court filing, the Army stored the material for more than two decades in two earth-covered magazines. Inspectors discovered in March that the chemical had deteriorated. Changes in its storage solution had allowed crystals to form, making the material more sensitive to shock and friction.
The EPA permit describes an imminent danger of accidental detonation. The Army insists that moving the drums would expose workers to unacceptable risks.
Officials spent months reviewing disposal options, and the EPA issued successive emergency storage permits before approving in-place detonation on November 13.
The plant’s regular hazardous-waste permit did not authorize treatment at the storage site. The new emergency permit also required monitoring and possible cleanup beyond the facility’s boundaries. Those safeguards did not satisfy the challengers.
That authorization took effect immediately. Yet the EPA published public notice on November 16, three days later and only four days before the planned blasts.
The Army’s November 15 advisory acknowledged that explosions would send lead particles into the air and onto the ground. It urged people in projected impact areas to stay inside, close windows, limit outdoor exposure and clean contaminated surfaces afterward.
The Army’s plume projections also shifted as weather forecasts changed. Initial maps showed potential lead contamination extending dozens of miles into Iowa and Illinois. Yet officials across the region complained of inadequate warning. The Illinois EPA acknowledged that its federal counterparts had not even notified it of the planned explosions.
The Lawsuit
The environmental organizations argue that the EPA approved a dangerous disposal method without adequate safeguards or sufficient examination of alternatives.
Their emergency motion invokes the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act and federal rules governing miscellaneous hazardous-waste treatment facilities. It accuses the agency of arbitrarily accepting the Army’s conclusions about the necessity of open detonation.
The groups point particularly to chemical neutralization, which could destroy the explosive without creating a blast plume. The Army rejected that approach because it would require extended handling of unstable containers. The challengers say officials have not publicly supplied enough evidence to justify that dismissal.
They also contest the permit’s provisions for soil, water, crops, livestock, testing, and cleanup. Although the document requires sampling before, during, and after detonation, they argue that the measures do not adequately cover the possible exposure area. They want stronger protections for children, farmers, and nearby water supplies. Their filing warns that lead dust could reach communities 100 miles away under certain conditions.
The health stakes are substantial. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says no safe blood lead level has been identified for children. Even modest exposure can impair learning and development.
Iowa Environmental Council counsel Michael Schmidt questioned whether officials seriously considered every alternative.
The Army Pushes Back
Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle announced Thursday that the military would delay the operation until Monday. He warned that falling temperatures could further destabilize the material and described detonation as the option posing the lowest overall risk.
On Friday, the Army, EPA, and Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) promised their most extreme safeguards to ensure “no risk to the public.” Yet the Army’s own advisory acknowledged that lead particles would settle on the ground.
But the Department of Justice (DOJ) raised a more consequential possibility.
In a November 20 court filing, federal lawyers pledged to oppose the environmental groups’ emergency motion by Sunday. They also cited a regulation allowing hazardous-waste treatment without an EPA permit in certain immediate emergencies.
Under that regulation, an explosives specialist must determine that an immediate threat requires an immediate response. Whether those conditions exist here remains contested.
That could become the government’s alternative legal route if the stay remains. But the filing did not announce that the Army would use the exception, nor did the court decide whether it would apply.
A Warning Across State Lines
Officials in Illinois are also demanding answers. In a Friday statement, state agencies said they still wanted the underlying plume-modeling data and details about federal monitoring. They warned that changing winds could send lead dust into western and central Illinois.
A bipartisan group of lawmakers had already urged the Army and EPA to delay the explosions, explore alternatives and explain the risks to farmland, families, and waterways.
Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds activated the state emergency operations center on Friday to coordinate preparations.
For now, the government faces two hazards: unstable explosives that cannot safely remain indefinitely, and the possibility of spreading toxic lead while destroying them.
The court has not solved that dilemma. It has required federal officials to confront the legal challenge before proceeding under their suspended permit.

sources.news_title: US Army tells court it intends to detonate bomb-making material in Iowa by Tuesday despite pause. Here’s what we know
sources.text:
The Justice Department on Sunday asked a federal appeals court to lift its pause on a permit allowing the US Army to detonate nearly five tons of material containing lead azide at an Iowa munitions plant, saying the Army intends to carry out the detonation Tuesday.
A federal appeals court temporarily paused the US Environmental Protection Agency permit on Thursday that would allow the Army to detonate the material at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in tiny Middletown after environmental groups sued. The Army, in coordination with the EPA, plans to destroy nearly 70 drums containing lead azide, a compound used to detonate munitions, the military branch said. The detonation, originally scheduled for Friday morning, had been moved to Monday before it was later moved to Tuesday.
The Army’s plan has drawn heavy pushback from concerned Iowans and politicians about the plume’s spread over a vast swath of Iowa, the Mississippi River and into parts of Illinois. Environmental groups suing the EPA said the Army had, as of late Sunday morning, failed to update the public about latest weather forecasts, as well as projections of the path of the plume containing lead dust. Lead exposure is unhealthy at any level, and it’s especially dangerous to children, health officials said.
As the legal fight has unfolded, the Justice Department in a filing late Saturday said the court’s order “does not enjoin or otherwise prohibit the Army from acting under a separate legal authority.” The Army says the degraded material could explode on its own as temperatures drop. “The real choice, in other words, is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned and mitigated detonation and an unplanned and unmitigated explosion,” the filing said.
Federal officials are now trying to bypass the judicial process and review while not showing they had pursued other safer alternatives than detonation, lawyers representing environmental groups argued.
“People across numerous impacted communities speaking up and demanding accountability is the only reason there was an opportunity to pause and think about better ways to approach the lead azide problem,” Thien Chau, a senior attorney at Earthjustice, which represents the environmental groups, said in a statement Sunday. “Yet despite claiming public safety is its top priority and public communication is essential to trust, the Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public’s demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm.”
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds on Friday activated a state emergency operations center, while officials in nearby Illinois are warning residents about dust spilling over into their state.
The Federal Aviation Administration has restricted flights around Middletown from Monday through Wednesday, according to a temporary flight restriction notice.
Here’s what we know about the planned detonation and the legal battle.
Army says detonation is needed
The Army in March, during “routine stockpile surveillance,” discovered lead azide housed in bunkers had been degrading, according to Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle. Officials evaluating the best way to dispose of the material communicated with “stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the modeled impact area about the danger it posed,” Telle said.
The lead azide’s degraded status left it “extremely unstable and sensitive to even slight friction or movement,” according to an FAQ distributed by the Army to the community last month. “Packing and transporting it poses an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation to personnel handling and transporting as well as to the public.”
After coordinating with the EPA, experts and the community, officials “determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area,” Telle said.
Army officials held an October 15 community meeting to share information about a potential detonation in late November, according to documents on the plant’s page. Then, on November 15, the community got a notice of a detonation on Friday, according to an Army news release.
After pushback, the Army rescheduled the detonation to Monday — the “latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material,” Telle said.
While noting the court’s pause is still in place, the City of Fort Madison said Saturday it was notified that the detonation would most likely occur either Monday or Tuesday, but if it doesn’t happen this week, “another time will need to be arranged with additional planning.” City officials said they hadn’t been given any further information but expect the state to issue more details on Sunday.
Waiting too long to detonate the lead azide could pose more hazards later, Telle said. The emergency permit from the EPA would allow the Army to do the detonation between November 13 and February 11, 2027.
The US Army has delayed plans to detonate several tons of unstable explosives at an Iowa ammunition plant amid concerns that the blasts could spread toxic lead particles into nearby communities. Residents have been advised to take precautions, while the Army says moving the chemicals could be even more dangerous.
Still, the problem should have been evaluated 20 years ago, said Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a University of Iowa professor and environmental health expert.
“Somebody left it to rot that long, for it to now being the only option is to blow it up on site because it can’t be moved,” he told CNN. “It’s regrettable, and it’s almost, it’s hard to believe that it’s happening in this country.”
O’Shaughnessy said the situation is “unprecedented” and called a planned detonation “the lesser of two evils.”
“They’re pretty much up against a wall here to get it done,” he told CNN’s Jessica Dean on Sunday. “It’s extremely unfortunate that it’s come to this, but I would agree that it’s better to be under a planned scenario than a random event that may occur under really bad meteorological conditions.”
The Army had previously awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based firm that uses chemicals to neutralize munitions, but later canceled the deal citing safety concerns, court filings show, as first reported by The New York Times, and instead opted to detonate the lead azide.
“This decision is supported by the technical consensus across military and federal explosive safety authorities that this is the only safe method of treatment,” read a partially redacted September letter included in the court filings from Amy L. Borman, deputy assistant secretary of the Army for Environment, Safety and Occupational Health.
CNN has reached out to the Army for comment.
Valentine Nzengung, a chief executive at MuniRem, told CNN the Army “told us that they evaluated reports and they found out that controlled detonation was the safest way, and that is why they were moving forward with controlled detonation. They did not provide us much more detail than this.”
Iowans and local officials push back
Officials at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant have regularly updated officials in Middletown – home to 363 people – about the planned detonation, according to Brieanna Beck, the city clerk and municipal officer, who said she has quickly shared each update on the city’s Facebook page. The city has been aware of the detonation plan for a couple of months, she told CNN in an email.
The Army plant sent letters to homes potentially affected by the detonation, Beck said.
The governor’s office and state agencies were coordinating with EPA and Army officials to “continuously monitor the situation and keep local partners informed,” Reynolds said Friday.
More than 80 miles north of Middletown, Cedar Rapids is preparing for the detonation. Officials in Iowa’s second-most populous city are taking steps to monitor the drinking water supply — drawn from wells along the Cedar River — for potential contamination, though they don’t anticipate impacts, according to a city update.
But plans and communication around the detonation have gotten strong pushback from environmental advocates, as well as state and federal politicians in Iowa and neighboring Illinois.
Officials in Iowa City, about 60 miles north of Middletown, said they didn’t know about the planned detonation until news began circulating early last week and were unaware of any state or federal agency formally notifying them, according to City Manager Geoff Fruin in a declaration on Saturday supporting the environmental groups’ lawsuit. An email Friday told the city an EPA team was deployed to collect a pre-detonation surface water sample because Iowa City, with a population of over 75,000 people, is within a 100-mile radius of the detonation, he said.
Iowa City officials have been discussing possible protocols to address impacts from the detonation, Fruin said. But he added it’s difficult to plan due to “lack of notice and information.”
Josh Turek, the US senator-elect for Iowa, has called for a delay to the detonation, saying he had “heard from many Iowans who are worried about their health and safety due to the potential risk of lead exposure as a result of the detonation.”
Rob Sand, the incoming governor, said Iowans’ safety now and in the future should be the government’s top concern. “An unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation,” he said. “The public deserves to know, if this is the safest option, why other options were worse.”
Parts of western and central Illinois could be affected by the lead plume under the current weather forecast, Illinois state officials said in an update Friday. Illinois health and environmental protection officials said they are monitoring the planned detonation and have issued updates to residents.
Illinois agriculture officials have issued guidance to protect livestock and pets. They recommended keeping animals inside until the plume has passed and washing them to remove potential contaminants. Meanwhile, officials warned of exposure through fishing.
Residents should stay indoors on the detonation day, with windows and doors closed for one to two days after as a precaution, Illinois officials said. They also encouraged people to use portable air cleaners equipped with a HEPA filter.
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said Friday he had spoken with Telle, urging more transparency about the planned detonation.
“The State is still seeking more data from them on how this could impact Illinoisans and is working to keep you informed and safe,” Pritzker said.
What the court has said
Environmental advocates sued the US EPA on Thursday over the emergency permit allowing the Army to detonate the lead azide, citing concerns about the potential impacts of the explosion.
The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals on Thursday temporarily stayed the EPA’s emergency permit until it rules on the groups’ emergency motion, but didn’t say when the court would take action on the case.
The Army, in a joint statement with the US Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA, said Friday afternoon, “The entire interagency is working together to ensure that the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa, is conducted in the safest fashion possible.”
“Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” the statement said, adding they will keep local officials and the public updated.
The cleanup requirements under the current permit are inadequate to properly address the scope and degree of potential impacts, according to Chau, the senior attorney at Earthjustice, who filed the lawsuit on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter.
There doesn’t appear to be sufficient understanding of how far the plume would spread, as well as which bodies of water, such as the Mississippi River, and land would be blanketed with lead dust, including where people live, Chau told reporters Friday.
Environmental advocates called on state leaders, including Reynolds, to take control of communication over the planned detonation.
“Iowans deserve a transparent, coordinated, and effective response to this unprecedented event,” Michael Schmidt, general counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, said in a news briefing.
The Justice Department first cited a federal regulation that exempts responses to an “immediate threat” to human health, public safety, property or the environment from EPA permitting requirements in its Friday filing. In Saturday’s filing, it said the Army intends to invoke that exemption. Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the Army’s 71st Ordnance Group, which handles explosive ordnance disposal, determined the lead azide poses “an immediate threat,” according to a sworn declaration filed with Saturday’s notice.
The Justice Department has not responded to CNN’s request for comment.
“We want to be absolutely clear that the regulation they cite is an extraordinary and extreme backstop for situations where there is truly nothing else that can be done,” Rachel Rintelmann, a managing attorney at Earthjustice, said in an email of the Friday filing. “It is an incredibly high bar, and we urge the Army not to rely on it if it is only doing so to sidestep the ongoing processes to obtain transparency and protections that communities, government leaders, and the law demand.”
Federal courts have the authority to prohibit the detonation, said Richard Revesz, a New York University School of Law professor who specializes in environmental and regulatory law and was an Office of Management and Budget official during the Biden administration.
Courts should carefully consider whether the Army is correct in its assertion that controlled detonation was the “option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area,” Revesz said in an email to CNN, citing Telle’s statement on the detonation. “The damage to the immediate and surrounding areas could be enormous and should not be disregarded merely on the basis of conclusory assertions.”
Health risks of lead exposure
There is no safe level of lead in the body, Dr. Sameer Vohra, director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, said in a statement. “(And) when inhaled or swallowed, it can pose serious health risks.”
With the detonation, the hope is if the lead azide spreads over a wider area, it won’t stay in high-level concentrations, according to O’Shaughnessy, the University of Iowa professor.
“It’s kind of like one of these, the solution to pollution is dilution, right?” he said.
There is the potential for exposure through the air during the initial plume or through touch after it has settled, he said, adding neither exposure is worse than the other because the lead will still build up in your body both ways.
Lead is toxic to the brain. Exposure is known to cause serious harm to children’s health, resulting in slowed growth and development, as well as problems with learning, behavior, hearing and speech, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Environmental advocates also warn the detonation could worsen health for residents in Iowa, which has the second-highest rate of cancer of any US state and is one of only three states where the rate is rising.
The local National Weather Service office forecasts cooler, drier conditions Tuesday, with highs in the upper 30s.
Wind conditions could affect how far lead particles travel. Wind speeds are expected near zero Tuesday, with weak winds blowing from north to south becoming near motionless by midday, CNN meteorologist Tyler Ory said.
CNN’s Holly Yan, Kara Devlin and Bill Kirkos contributed to this report.

sources.text:
Groups Respond to Army’s Plan to Proceed with Lead Azide Detonation in Iowa
posted on Sunday, November 22, 2026 in Council News
Important: IEC strongly recommends that all Iowans and anyone in the path of a potential plume remain vigilant and continue to monitor updates from the U.S. Army and your local officials, as it is likely the detonation will proceed on Monday, November 23. Continue to check this site for updates: https://www.army.mil/asc#org-iowa-army-ammunition-plant
St. Louis, MO and Des Moines, IA—The Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club, and Earthjustice will continue to advocate for accountability from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Army in the planned detonation of lead azide in Middletown, Iowa. Early Sunday morning, the groups filed declarations with the court that call out the Army’s inadequate public notice and information and question the Army’s and EPA’s claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration.
The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a statement with the court late on Saturday, Nov. 21, indicating that the Army intends to invoke emergency provisions of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) to detonate 9,773.5 pounds of lead azide stored at the Iowa Army Ammunitions Plant without a permit from the EPA. According to the DOJ’s statement, the Army intends to do so no later than Nov. 24.
This emergency is of the Army’s own making. The Army has not publicly provided details about why the lead azide was not disposed of before it became so dangerous.
The Army’s own storage and inspection practices allowed a primary explosive to sit until it reportedly degraded to the point that any alternative disposal method is now deemed too dangerous. The lack of transparency raises real questions about the scope and extent of potential impacts.
“The new information from the DOJ indicates that the problem is significantly worse than the Army originally shared. It appears that detonation may be, at this point, the only feasible option due to how long this problem was allowed to persist. The public deserves to know immediately which communities will be impacted and how residents can most effectively protect themselves and mitigate impacts on their health and homes,” said Michael Schmidt, General Counsel for the Iowa Environmental Council.
The Army knew about this stockpile of dangerous munitions waste for years, and it knew since at least March that the material was becoming unstable. Yet, just one week ago, most Iowans — including those directly in the path of a toxic lead plume, the Iowa governor, and key state agencies and officials – were unaware the Army intended to detonate nearly five tons of lead azide.
The environmental groups argue the EPA and Army permitting documents have not demonstrated nor provided appropriate documentation that all other safer alternatives to mitigate the material were thoroughly explored.
“People across numerous impacted communities speaking up and demanding accountability is the only reason there was an opportunity to pause and think about better ways to approach the lead azide problem,” said Earth Justice Attorney Thien Chau. “Yet despite claiming public safety is its top priority and public communication is essential to trust, the Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public’s demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm.”
As of 11:00 a.m. Central Time on Sunday, Nov. 22, the Army has failed to provide the public with updated weather modeling and mapping showing the path of the lead dust plume, which means people impacted have little time to take precautions to protect their families and homes. The wind patterns have shifted significantly, which means that potential community exposures have likely changed without visible effort by the Army to provide updated information to the public.
“The Army has clearly mishandled this situation, and Iowans and residents in our neighboring states deserve a full review of all of the missteps that led us to this point. However, if detonation is now the only option, it is imperative that everyone impacted has access to the full range of testing, mitigation, and remediation resources,” said Wally Taylor, Attorney and Legal Chair for the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter.
See previous news releases about the detonation plan in our Newsroom.

The Iowa Environmental Council is the state’s largest and most comprehensive environmental alliance, comprised of diverse organizations and individuals working together to protect Iowa’s natural environment. Through education, advocacy, and coalition-building, the Council raises awareness, generates action, and creates large-scale change. In addition to protecting every person’s right to get outdoors and access the healing power of nature, the Sierra Club works to promote clean energy, safeguard the health of our communities, protect wildlife, and preserve our remaining wild places through grassroots activism, public education, lobbying, and legal action.
Earthjustice is the premier nonprofit public interest environmental law organization. We wield the power of law and the strength of partnership to protect people’s health, to preserve magnificent places and wildlife, to advance clean energy, and to combat climate change. The United States Army issued a statement late Saturday night indicating it will go on with the planned demolition of lead azide in Middletown.
Five tons of the increasingly unstable explosive are sitting at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. Inspectors have said the best option for disposing of the lead azide is to blow it up before it explodes on its own. But that would create a lead-laden cloud that would drift over portions of Eastern Iowa.
Officials warn the dropping temperatures combined with the doors to the holding facility being removed for the planned explosion have made the material even more unstable and susceptible to an uncontrolled detonation.
